                       ARGUMENTS OF PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY OF OKLAHOMA

                COMES NOW Public Service Company of Oklahoma (“PSO”), by and through the
         undersigned counsel, and files legal arguments to address

                                                  INTRODUCTION

                 The Commission’s Rules of Practice provide “A written or oral statement by or a
         communication from any person . . . may be received without cross-examination but will be
         considered only as argument …”1 A “person” means, among other entities, a corporation. 2 PSO is
         a corporation that provides Commission rate regulated electric utility service to over 580,000
         customers located in over 55 counties in the state of Oklahoma. PSO is currently addressing many
         of the same large-load tariff issues that are the subject matter of this proceeding in Case No. PUD
         2025-000075.
                                             PROCEDURAL POSTURE

                 Rather than opening a Notice of Inquiry (NOI) to address the legality of customers
         obtaining their own generation supply and requiring a utility to transport that electric service to
         the customer located in the service territory of that utility, the Commission has chosen to address
         the legal issues in separate dockets involving two electric utilities. The process chosen by the
         Commission excludes other utilities such as rural electric cooperative (REC), generation and
         transmission cooperatives (G&T), municipal utilities, The Empire District Electric Company (the
         third investor-owned electric utility in the state), and municipalities that have franchise agreements
         with rate regulated utilities that may be adversely impacted by a Commission decision in this
         docket or PSO’s docket. Both cases are addressing the legality of what has been termed Bring
         Your Own New Generation (BYONG). The current two case approach is a departure from the past
         commission practice of opening an NOI to address an important issue that all utilities, as well as
         other entities, should have an opportunity in which to participate.

                                                           ARGUMENTS

                     I.       THE COMMISSION SHOULD MAKE A DETERMINATION AS TO WHAT
                              THE TERM “WHEELING” MEANS.

         The BYONG proposals have introduced the concept of an integrated electric public utility
         transporting power generated by another supplier to a facility located in OG&E’s and PSO’s
         respective service territories. The electric utility industry has used the term “wheeling” to describe
         that process. The American Bar Association Utility Section Newsletter has produced a glossary of
         terms for the utility industry (electric, gas and telecommunications). The term “Wheeling” is
         defined as follows:

                             “Movement of electricity on the Transmission system of a utility for
                             some party other than that utility; a Transmission service for
                             others.”3

               PSO believes the Commission should adopt that definition and, at the next Chapter 35 rule
         making, add the definition of Wheeling to the Commission’s Electric Rules.

                    II       THE COMMISSION SHOULD MAKE A DETERMINATION THAT BYONG
                             AS PROPOSED IS A RETAIL SALE OF POWER.

                  In both the present case (“OG&E case”) and Case PUD 2025-000075 (“PSO case”) there
         is testimony and claims by the proponents of BYONG that the described transactions are wholesale
         transactions. However, the BYONG proposals do not meet the definition of wholesale transactions
         under Oklahoma law.

                The Commission need only decide if the BYONG involves an electric supplier providing
         power to another electric supplier for resale to the customer to determine if the transaction(s) are
         wholesale transactions. Oklahoma law (17 O.S. §158.22(4)) defines wholesale service as “electric
         energy furnished by an electric supplier to another electric supplier for resale.” Retail Service is
         defined under Oklahoma law as “electric service furnished to a consumer for ultimate
         consumption” and specifically excludes anything defined as wholesale service. 17 O.S. §
         158.22(4). Federal law (16 U.S.C. 824 (d)) defines a wholesale transaction as “a sale of electric
         energy to any person for resale.”

                 Both Oklahoma law and Federal law require that to be considered a wholesale transaction,
         one electric supplier must provide the power to another electric supplier for resale to the ultimate
         consumer. None of the BYONG proposals in either the OG&E or PSO cases meet the legal
         definition of a wholesale transaction.

                PUD witness Scalf suggested in his sur-rebuttal testimony that the Commission consider
         approving what could only be considered a sham transaction by requiring OG&E to purchase a
         customer’s selected supplier’s power and sell to the customer at cost. 4 It appears PUD is ignoring

         the longtime of Oklahoma Supreme Court decisions regarding the inability of the Commission to
         take on the role of utility management. See e.g. Lone Star Gas Co. v. Corporation Commission,
         1934 OK 396 (holding that the powers of the Commission “do not extend to an invasion of the
         discretion vested in the corporate management. [They do] not include the power to approve or
         disapprove contracts about to be entered into nor to approve or veto the expenditures proposed.”
         It would appear that PUD is desperate to find a way to change a retail transaction into a wholesale
         transaction. PUD’s recommendation is regulatory alchemy.

              The facts in both the OG&E and PSO cases would have the utility transport electricity for some
         party other than the utility for an end use customer. There would be no resell by the incumbent
         utility. The only conclusion that can be reached is that the proposed BYONG is retail wheeling.
         Under no construction of Oklahoma or Federal law could such a transaction be construed as
         wholesale.

                 III.     ONCE THE COMMISSION HAS DETERMINED THAT BYONG IS RETAIL
                          WHEELING, THE COMMISSION MUST DETERMINE IF OKLAHOMA LAW
                          ALLOWS RETAIL WHEELING.

                 PSO agrees with OG&E’s legal analysis that the Oklahoma Legislature has enacted a
         statutory mandate5 that prohibits third-party retail electric service absent a statutory exemption.
         The BYONG proponents recognize this prohibition against third-party retail providers. To escape
         statutory prohibition, the proponents of retail wheeling have invented (and advocate the
         Commission adopt) a legal fantasy that they claim turns their transaction into a wholesale
         transaction, even though there is no resale by an electric supplier.6

                 The legal fantasy includes attempts to either ignore, or change, statutory definitions of
         “retail electric supplier” and “retail electric service” to avoid the true identity of their proposed
         BYONG transaction. However, a legitimate view of their proposal demonstrates that it is a direct
         sale of electric power to a consumer located in the utility’s service territory.7 In other words it is
         a retail transaction, and without question, Oklahoma has a statutory prohibition on the sale of
         electricity for ultimate consumption except by those defined as public utilities by the State.

                 IV.      THE COMMISSION MUST ABIDE BY THE LEGISLATURE’S DIRECTIVE
                          FOUND AT 17 O.S.190.4 (A) TO REFRAIN FROM “ISSUING ANY ORDERS
                          RELATING TO THE RESTRUCTURING OF OKLAHOMA’S ELECTRIC
                          UTILITY INDUSTRY WITHOUT PRIOR EXPRESS AUTHORIZATION BY
                          THE OKLAHOMA STATE LEGISLATURE.”

                The brief submitted by OG&E describes the history of the Electric Restructuring Act of
         1997 (Restructuring Act), including the reasons why the legislature rejected the concept as not
         being in the public interest. One of the “primary goals of a restructured electric utility industry”

         was “to encourage the development of a competitive electricity industry through the unbundling
         of prices and services and separation of generation services from transmission and distribution
         services” (emphasis supplied).8

                 The separation of generation services is the very core to those advocating for BYONG. The
         legislature has specifically prohibited the Commission from “issuing any orders relating” to
         restructuring without prior express authorization by the Oklahoma Legislature (emphasis
         supplied).9 Approving the proposed BYONG would be an order approving the separation of
         generation services from transmission and distribution services without specific legislative
         approval. Therefore an order approving the BYONG proposal would be contrary to Oklahoma
         law.

                 The Commission is “a tribunal of limited jurisdiction,” possessing “only the authority
         expressly stated or necessary by implication.”10 The Restructuring Act has expressly stated that
         the Commission is without authority to separate generation from transmission and distribution.
         The Oklahoma Legislature did not expressly authorize the Commission to separate generation
         from transmission and distribution in the recently passed Data Center Customer Ratepayer
         Protection Act of 2026 (Protection Act).11 An order approving a BYONG proposal that would
         separate generation from transmission and distribution requires further action of the legislature.
